title: The finger and the moon
hook: a finger pointing at the moon is not the moon: words point, they are not the thing (Lankavatara)

segments.voice: Yesterday, worlds in a speck of dust, and ages in one moment. Your line: a world in a grain. What small thing did you stop and look at? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

Someone stands in a dark yard, points up and says: look, the moon. And the person next to them stares hard at the end of the finger. Fingernail. Knuckle. A little ink stain. It's a small joke. The Lankavatara Sutra uses it to say something serious about every word of teaching, its own words included. And it's a good way to end this week. Today: the finger and the moon.
screen: `LOOK, THE MOON.` → `STARING AT THE FINGER.` → `ABOUT EVERY WORD OF TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, as the Lankavatara gives it. When someone points out the moon with a fingertip, a foolish person looks at the fingertip and not at the moon. In the same way, the sutra says, people who cling to the letter of the teaching, to the words alone, don't see the truth the words are pointing at. Two things are true at once here. First, the finger is needed. Without someone pointing, nobody looks up. The sutra isn't telling anyone to throw words away. Teachings, texts, explanations: they're how anyone finds the direction at all. Second, the finger is not the moon. A person can learn every word, repeat every line, argue every point, and still be staring at a knuckle. The Lankavatara comes back to this difference between the words and the meaning. Words are useful. They are not the thing. Some later Chan and Zen teachers picked up the image too. Now look back at this week, because it has been a week of fingers. On the first day, a goddess switched bodies with Sariputra, pointing at labels that aren't fixed. Then Vimalakirti pointed with silence. Then a net of jewels. A young man walking from teacher to teacher. A tower full of towers. A world in a grain. Each one is a finger, aimed somewhere. None of them is the moon. They're there so the eyes can travel past them. The test is small: after hearing something wise, does the attention stay on the clever words, or move on to what they were pointing at?
screen: `A FOOL LOOKS AT THE FINGERTIP.` · `THE FINGER IS NEEDED.` · `THE FINGER IS NOT THE MOON.` · `A WEEK OF FINGERS.` · then, large: `NOT THE FINGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: point at the moon, then look. If you can see the sky, point at it. If not, point at a lamp, a window, anything with light. Hold the finger there for a breath and look at the finger itself. Then let your eyes move past it, to what it's pointing at. Lower the hand. Keep looking. Now let the word for the thing go too: not lamp, not sky, just this light, this color, here. Rest there and breathe. If a word comes back, notice it, and look past it again. The bell holds the time.
The finger and the moon. The Lankavatara's picture of words as a finger pointing: needed, but never the thing itself. Today's word.
screen: `THE FINGER AND THE MOON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the finger. Today, when a phrase sounds wise, ask what it's pointing at, and go look. A body, a silence, a net, a road, a tower, a grain: that was the week. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers, and especially Chan and Zen teachers, use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras and explanations point toward awakening and are not awakening itself.

notes: Passage paraphrased; no public-domain English translation used (Suzuki 1932 not used). Confirm the wording 'a foolish person looks at the fingertip and not at the moon' as a paraphrase, and the application to clinging to the letter of the teaching.
'Buddhist sutras tell it more than once' refers to the Lankavatara and the Surangama (which has its own finger-and-moon passage); confirm or soften.
'Later Chan and Zen teachers picked up the image and kept it close' is a general reception claim; confirm or soften.
Week-end look back covers days 1191–1196 (Sariputra transformed, thunderous silence, Indra's net, Sudhana, Maitreya's tower, the grain); confirm day 1191 framing once that script exists.
Original: चन्द्र (candra), moon; the Lankavatara's Sanskrit may use candra or śaśin. Confirm.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'sutras tell it more than once' count claim and softened 'keeps returning' and the Chan/Zen reception claim to 'some later teachers'; removed the 'on an ordinary day' stock turn.
